The screen

Every image below is the browser tool itself, captured at 2x from a live session against a real Zerodha feed. Nothing here is a mockup. The account name, email and Zerodha client ID are masked and the owner-only Admin menu item is hidden; those are the only edits.

They were taken after the close, so the header reads Market closed and the day's total is zero. The market map is the one exception: after the close every member reads flat, so it is from an earlier live session. The signal, the levels and every indicator reading are the real ones from that session; nothing was put into a demo mode to be photographed.

How it is laid out

On a computer the sections sit in a rail down the left: Home and the Signal, then the chart, the option chain, the market map, market pulse, sector scope and momentum spikes, the analysis tabs, news and your record. Your account and the date your access renews are at the foot of the rail. On a phone the rail is a drawer behind the menu button at the top, and Home, Signal, Chart and the option chain sit in a bar along the bottom within reach of a thumb.

The few things that are switches rather than places — index points against option premium, the lot count, whether the tool keeps running when the page is shut — sit beside what they affect instead of behind a menu.

Reading the signal board

PartWhat it is telling you
Signal ticketthe call itself — BUY CE, BUY PE, or nothing. OPEN means it is live and tracked; PREVIEW means a direction exists but no ticket was issued. When something is holding the entry, the badge says which: CONFIRMING, COOLDOWN, POSITION OPEN, DAY LIMIT, MARKET OPENING, CLOSING AUCTION or MARKET CLOSED.
Entry / Nowthe premium at issue, and the premium now. The rupee figure beside them is that difference across your chosen lots.
Reward : riskhow far the market has room to run, divided by the distance to the stop. Below the floor it never became a ticket at all. It is not what the exit pays — that is in the Risk and reward panel.
T1 / T2 / T3the three targets, each with how far price has travelled toward it — a check mark and a timestamp once reached.
Stopwith the same progress bar, which is the one you actually want to be watching.
The percentage beside each levelthe chance of the index touching it before the 15:30 close (on Bitcoin, within the next 24 hours), from the option chain’s implied volatility and calibrated against past trades. The chances overlap — a trade can touch a target and still hit the stop — so they do not add up to 100 and are not a win rate.
Risk and rewardunder the ladder: what the stop costs and what each target makes, in rupees at your lot count after Zerodha’s charges, how many times the risk each target is, and the win rate the trade needs to break even.
Skip cooldownappears while a cooldown is the only thing holding a ticket. It lifts the wait once; every other check still has to pass, and a ticket issued that way is marked in the trade log.
Holding overnightin the last hour, an open ticket shows what carrying the position past the close would cost in time decay before the next session — three nights over a weekend — and what buying into the close did in a three-year test. The tool closes its own ticket at the bell.
Confidencethe dial, with every input that fed it listed underneath. A dash means that input abstained and was ignored rather than counted as neutral.
Market trendthe plain-English label — RANGE-BOUND / CHOPPY, MODERATE DOWNTREND — with the ADX reading and how far price has actually displaced in ATR terms.
Sessioneverything closed today, in order, with the running total split into booked and open.

Every section, and what it tells you

The Signal is where a trade is decided. The other sections are there to check it against: what the rest of the market is doing, what the options are pricing, and what has happened before. None of them issues a ticket.

Market

SectionWhat it shows
ChartFifteen-minute candles, or five-minute and daily, with the 20 and 50 EMAs and a VWAP weighted by the index future’s real volume. A live signal’s T1, T2, T3 and stop are drawn as lines. Beside it, today’s range: where price sits between the day’s low and high.
Option chainThe option clock: how open interest changed at each strike within a time window you choose, read from the tool’s own recording of the chain. It is change within the window, not OI added today — positions closing count as much as positions opening. Below it, the chain around the money: last price, bid, ask, spread and open interest for calls and puts.
MarketThe index mover: how many index points each member added or took away today, the five pushing hardest and the five dragging most. Then every member with its sector, weight and move.
Market pulseHow many members are up against down, and four screens across them: members breaking a 10-day high or low, a 50-day high or low, trading on volume well above their 20-session average, and sitting nearest their 50-day extreme. On Bitcoin, which has no members, it reads open interest across the live option chain instead.
Sector scopeThe market map — every member sized by its weight and coloured by its move, so you can see whether an index is carried by two heavyweights or moving as a whole — and each sector’s weighted move today.
Momentum spikesThe members that moved most over the last five and ten minutes, with their volume against their own average for that time of day. After the close it shows the session’s final minutes, and says so.

Analysis · Indian indices only

SectionWhat it shows
VolatilityIndia VIX against the volatility the index actually delivered over 20 sessions. When implied sits above realised, options are expensive for the movement they are getting — that favours the seller and costs the buyer, and it says nothing about direction. Also: where VIX sits in its year, the expected move over a day, a week and to expiry, how often the index really stayed inside its one-day band, and a volatility cone ranking each window against its own year.
Greeks & IVImplied volatility across the strikes — puts usually dearer than calls, because protection costs more than upside. The chain priced with delta, gamma, theta per day and vega, and where the chain’s gamma is concentrated once weighted by open interest. It shows where that gamma sits, not who holds it: that is not visible from outside the exchange, so it is not claimed.
LevelsFloor pivots — S2, S1, the pivot, R1, R2 — from the previous session’s high, low and close, with ATR(14): the distance the index typically covers in a day, which is what a stop has to survive. And the opening range, with whether price has closed above, below or inside it.
InternalsWhat the index members are doing underneath the index: how many are above their 20- and 50-day averages, advancing against declining, at new highs or lows, and the advance/decline line over 20 sessions. An index can rise while most of its members fall; a falling line under a steady index means fewer names are carrying it.
Relative strengthThe members leading and lagging over the last 20 sessions. In a falling market the leader can still be down — it is only falling least.
SeasonalityThe average move by weekday, with how often each day closed up, the spread and the number of sessions behind it. The spread is wider than every average in the table, which is the point: these are tendencies, not rules. And the opening gaps — how often the index opened up, down or flat, and by how much.

Research

SectionWhat it shows
NewsMarket headlines, gathered in one place so you can check whether a move has a reason before you trade against it.
RecordA position calculator that turns your capital, your risk per trade, the entry and the stop into a lot count; a recap of the session; your track record — every ticket closed, wins and losses, from the trade file, with nothing left out; and “Why”, every input behind the current reading in full sentences.

On Bitcoin the Chart, Option chain, Market pulse, Momentum spikes, News and Record work the same way; the index-member and India VIX sections do not apply to a market of one instrument, and are hidden rather than shown empty.

Not investment advice. TradePicker is a decision-support screen that applies a fixed, published rule set to index data. It is not the output of a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or Investment Adviser, no recommendation is being made to any person, and no order is ever placed by this software. Trading index options can lose you your entire capital. The rule set was measured across three years of history and returned a negative expectancy after costs — the figures are here. You are responsible for anything you do with what you see.
TradePicker

A rule-based second opinion on Nifty, Bank Nifty and Sensex index options. It shows its working, it says WAIT most of the time, and it places no orders.
